record.title: OpenAI releases country-level work-activity classifications of consumer ChatGPT use
record.summary: OpenAI Economic Research released Signals v3.0, a public dataset and methodology describing consumer ChatGPT messages classified into work activities mapped to 165 O*NET Intermediate Work Activities across nearly 100 countries. Quarterly series span Q1 2025–Q3 2026. OpenAI reports that, across 74 countries observed in every quarter, the ten most common activities accounted for an average 51.1% of classified work messages in Q3 2026, down from 56.0% in Q1 2025. The dataset covers individual consumer plans, not enterprise messages or Codex; the work and activity labels are automated model classifications. The release measures message mix, not employment, task completion, productivity or labor-market effects.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: OpenAI Economic Research announced and documented Signals v3.0, a public release of aggregated ChatGPT work-use data and its methodology on 26 October 2026.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: OpenAI reports that, among 74 countries observed in every quarter, the ten most common work activities represented an average 51.1% of classified work messages in Q3 2026, compared with 56.0% in Q1 2025. Recalculation from the released CSV reproduces these rounded shares by averaging each country’s top-ten IWA total across the fixed 74-country panel; the released file and underlying classifications remain provider-supplied.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The release documentation describes quarterly country-level work-activity categories mapped to 165 O*NET Intermediate Work Activities; the dataset excludes enterprise messages and Codex, and its work-relatedness and activity labels are inferred by automated classifiers.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The release does not establish changes in employment, job displacement, worker productivity, task completion, or economy-wide AI adoption.

evidence_gaps.description: The linked CSV ZIP was downloaded and its 74-country top-ten statistic was reproduced from the released table. This verifies the published aggregation arithmetic only; the provider-generated sample and classifications have not been independently validated.
The work-relatedness and O*NET activity labels are inferred by OpenAI classifiers; independent labeling accuracy and cross-country/temporal comparability were not established.
The message-share series does not establish worker counts, employment-weighted task prevalence, task completion, productivity or labor-market effects.

brief.importance_rationale: If independently validated and used alongside labor data, a broad task-level cross-country usage series could materially improve measurement of where consumer AI is used at work and how that mix changes. The consequence is meaningful for economic research, but this release does not itself measure jobs, productivity or labor-market effects.
limitations: All described data and results are from OpenAI, the provider being measured; no independent audit or reproduction was found in this review.
The sample covers individual consumer ChatGPT, excludes enterprise messages and Codex, and excludes some account groups; it is not a census of AI use or work.
Work-relatedness and O*NET activity categories are automated model inferences from message context, not worker self-reports; classification error and drift may affect comparisons.
Message shares do not measure distinct workers, jobs, completed tasks, productivity, employment changes or causal AI effects.

Version 3.0 adds July–September 2026 and increases historical samples from 300,000 to 1,000,000 messages/month; earlier periods have been restated across releases and the dictionary documents cumulative privacy budgets.

The released CSV arithmetic reproduces the reported fixed-panel statistic, but this is not an independent validation of OpenAI’s source sample, differential-privacy processing or automated work/IWA classifications.

relationships.summary: Both are provider-authored AI-use data resources, but Google/MIT examines scientific workflows while OpenAI Signals v3 classifies consumer ChatGPT work-use messages across countries; their populations and measures are not directly comparable.

Quarterly series span Q1 2025–Q3 2026. OpenAI reports that, across 74 countries observed in every quarter, the ten most common activities accounted for an average 51.1% of classified work messages in Q3 2026, down from 56.0% in Q1 2025. The dataset covers individual consumer plans, not enterprise messages or Codex; the work and activity labels are automated model classifications. technical.claimed_result: OpenAI reports a lower concentration of classified work-related messages in the ten most common activities across a fixed panel of 74 countries between Q1 2025 and Q3 2026.
technical.compute_or_cost: No model training or compute cost; this is an observational dataset release.
technical.demonstrated_result: OpenAI's current data-download page still links the CSV archive and data dictionary under CC BY 4.0. The existing primary artifact receipt S4 records retrieval and inspection of the released archive and reproduction of the 74-country fixed-panel top-ten averages. This reproduces OpenAI's released-file arithmetic only; it does not independently validate the message sample or automated classifications.
technical.implementation_status: OpenAI continues to expose downloadable aggregated CSV files and a data dictionary under CC BY 4.0; its page invites researchers to combine these activity shares with other economic indicators. The separate data audit recorded in source S4 retrieved and inspected the archive. Work-relatedness and activity labels remain provider-generated, and the release does not itself measure productivity or employment outcomes.
technical.mechanism: OpenAI describes sampling consumer ChatGPT messages monthly, automatically classifying de-identified messages, mapping work-related messages to O*NET Intermediate Work Activities, aggregating them by country and quarter, and applying differential-privacy noise and release thresholds.
technical.novelty: The v3 release adds country-quarter work-activity categories mapped to 165 O*NET IWAs and extends the time series through Q3 2026, while increasing the documented monthly sample for prior periods.
technical.regime: Signals v3.0 documentation describes monthly samples of 1,000,000 consumer ChatGPT messages from Jul 2024 through Sep 2026, with the new O*NET activity series quarterly from Q1 2025 through Q3 2026. Enterprise messages and Codex are excluded.
technical.reproducibility: The data-download page and dictionary are currently accessible and link the public CSV. The prior S4 artifact audit records the archive hash, schema, fixed-panel calculation and reproduced rounded statistic. This is reproducibility of the published aggregation, not independent validation of OpenAI's source sample, classifier accuracy or population representativeness.
technical.strongest_baseline: The provider compares its own classified activity shares in Q1 2025 against Q3 2026 for the same 74-country panel; this is not an external or employment-weighted baseline.

brief.title: OpenAI releases country-level work-activity classifications of consumer ChatGPT use
brief.why_it_matters: A cross-country, task-level time series could help researchers compare consumer AI use with occupational and economic datasets. Its value depends on classifier validity, sampling and interpretation: message shares are not workers or jobs, and the provider-reported concentration trend does not demonstrate productivity or employment change.

related.summary: Both are provider-authored AI-use data resources, but Google/MIT examines scientific workflows while OpenAI Signals v3 classifies consumer ChatGPT work-use messages across countries; their populations and measures are not directly comparable.

other.title: Google, DeepMind and MIT FutureTech report early evidence on AI use and bottlenecks in science
other.summary: A Google, Google DeepMind and MIT FutureTech report combines an approximately 15-million-interaction sample from Google AI products, a curated analysis of 2,690 specialized scientific AI models and a survey of 637 active researchers in the United States and United Kingdom. The authors report that nearly half of surveyed scientists use AI daily; about three quarters report time savings averaging almost seven hours a week, much of which they say returns to research. They also report growing backlogs of untested hypotheses and substantial time spent checking AI outputs. These are early, author-reported findings based partly on self-report and Google-only interaction data; the study does not demonstrate causal productivity gains or increased scientific discoveries.
